paragraphs: The Hayden Heritage Center, with the Colorado Department of Transportation, manages the Mt. Harris Memorial on Highway 40 at the former town site. Former residents built the memorial. Mount Harris was founded in 1914 when the Colorado-Utah Coal Company bought the land. Brothers George and Byron Harris, from Iowa, developed the camp, which the center calls a model coal camp with wide, tree-lined streets, a cottonwood playground, a baseball park, and a rock business block.

Three mines employed the town. The Harris mine ran from 1914 to 1958, with entries on the south side of the river. The Wadge Mine, opened in 1887 by James and Sarah Wadge, was bought by Victor American Fuel Company in 1917 and ran until 1951. On January 27, 1942, an explosion there killed 34 miners. The Wolf Creek, later Pinnacle-Kemmerer or PK, mine operated until 1942. On May 20, 1958, the town was auctioned. Buildings were moved or demolished. The center says foundations and remnants remain. The museum at 300 W. Pearl Street in Hayden keeps an exhibit and holds a cleanup each spring and a biannual Mt. Harris Day.

paragraphs: The Flume’s October 18, 2013, account of a Park County Historical Society tour says Christ of the Rockies was built between 1930 and 1934. The statue is 33 feet high on a 22-foot base. The body is a steel frame with terra-cotta robe tiles fired and glazed in Denver, brought up by train, and carried to the site. Concrete was poured into the frame and the tiles attached. Mullen plot at Mount Olivet Cemetery near Golden. The Flume says John and Mary Dower bought the 160-acre former Cassells resort in 1929, near Shawnee. After Mary Dower died in 1952 the property passed to the Mary Dower Benevolent Corp. In 2007 the Boulder YMCA took over camp operations. On the 2013 tour, 20 people hiked 1.5 miles and more than 427 feet from camp, from about 8,437 feet to 8,864 feet at the statue base. paragraphs: GOCA at UCCS says Starr Kempf (1917–1995) built elaborate steel wind sculptures from the late 1970s, each taking up to three years. paragraphs: The National Sculptors’ Guild dates its placement of Snapshot in Lakewood’s Addenbrooke Park to June 15, 1994, and calls it placement number 6. The guild says Michael Jackson originally commissioned the multi-figure bronze. Children sit on a bench with a wagon at one side, holding toys and a soda, including a pouting child in back. The guild says the scene was inspired by photographs Jackson gave DeDecker.

A 2009 Denver Post passage quoted on that guild page says the Lakewood bronze is life-size, by Loveland artist Jane DeDecker, and was commissioned in 1992. It identifies the children as a young Jackson with friends made younger for the piece, including Macaulay Culkin, Gary Coleman, Janet Jackson, Brandi Jackson, and Brett Ratner, plus friends of the artist. Jackson’s original stood in the Neverland sculpture garden. Lakewood bought another cast in 1994 as the city’s first public artwork and, DeDecker told the Post, did not know about the Jackson connection at the time. She put a baseball glove on the young Jackson figure’s left hand.

paragraphs: The Colorado Italian American Foundation says the monument was conceived in 1892 by Hector Chiariglione and Columbo Delliquadri and unveiled on October 12, 1905. It calls the work an Italian stonemason-cut monument with a solid brass bust, and also says Italian sculptor Pietro Piai created the bronze bust, J.A. Byre engraved the pedestal, and CF&I stonemason Michele Albo set the foundation. The foundation’s 2025 anniversary program uses the address Columbus Monument, 100 E. Abriendo Ave., Pueblo, Colorado 81004, across from Rawlings Library. The foundation’s page calls it the first and last remaining Columbus monument west of the Mississippi.

The National Archives description on DocsTeach, drawn from National Register nomination materials, says Pietro Piai was the sculptor and Genest & Markert the contractor. It was unveiled in 1905, stands nearly 20 feet tall, and has a 5-foot bust in fifteenth-century Italian dress. The pedestal has Italian inscriptions from 1905, later English inscriptions, an eagle crest, and globes of the two hemispheres. DocsTeach also notes that in August 2020 Pueblo hired a mediator in a dispute over removal, and that in October 2020 the statue was vandalized with red paint. The City of Pueblo cultural-resources inventory lists “The Christopher Columbus Monument” at 100 West Abriendo Avenue, with a May 23, 2011 date and state site number 5PE.3162. Because the foundation says East Abriendo and the city inventory says West Abriendo, this guide does not pick a single side of the avenue.

paragraphs: The Colorado Sun reported on November 22, 2021, that friends installed a memorial to Warren Barnes on November 20, 2021. Barnes, 69, was known as the reading man because he sat in a breezeway off Main Street with a book, near the back entrance to Monique’s Bridal. Ironworker Tim Navin, of Sparks Fly Studio in Fruita, spent 285 hours on the piece. It has an iron tree bent as if by a south wind, a metal chair, and a sheet-metal book titled “And You Also,” the reply Barnes gave when people told him to have a good day. The memorial also says “Warren was here.”

The Sun says Barnes was killed in February 2021 while he slept under an elevated roadway near downtown. The person accused of killing him told investigators he chose a homeless person he thought no one would miss. Monique Lanotti told the Sun she used to set Barnes’s chair in the sun behind the bridal shop, where he read paperback thrillers and Louis L’Amour westerns and fed birds. Navin placed the sculpture between a bookstore and the bridal shop.
